sec.title: Background
sec.p: Wheat streak mosaic disease, caused by wheat streak mosaic virus (WSMV), is considered a serious cereal disease that threatens wheat yield worldwide. To date, only a limited number of genes related to WSMV resistance have been characterized. Identification of novel sources of resistance is essential for the development of resistant varieties.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: In this study a genome-wide association study (GWAS) and expression analysis of candidate QTLs through RT-qPCR were implemented on a set of 175 globally diverse wheat genotypes. A GWAS of 21,773 high-quality DArTseq markers revealed 17 significant markers (p-value < 10− 4, and FDR < 0.05) on chromosomes 1B, 2 A, 2B, 2D, 3 A, 3B, 4B, 5 A, 5B, 6 A, 6B, 6D and 7 A. GWAS results revealed some potential candidate genes for WSMV resistance, including several nucleotide binding site-leucine-rich repeats (NBS-LRR)-type resistance genes, different types of kinases such as serine-threonine/tyrosine-protein kinase and defense-related proteins such as F-box proteins (FBPs), GroEL-like heat shock protein 60 and cytochrome P450. Moreover, comparisons of the expression profiles of eight candidate genes between two accession, resistant (the landrace IPK41079) and susceptible (the cultivar Alamut), using RT-qPCR revealed higher relative expression levels in resistant than susceptible accessions.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: These candidate genes and associated QTLs represent promising targets for marker-assisted selection (MAS) following independent validation in additional wheat populations and field environments.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Bread wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) is one of the most important food crops for human nutrition. Wheat streak mosaic virus (WSMV) is considered as a devastating cereal virus worldwide, which causes significant losses in wheat production [1]. The WSMV belongs to the genus Tritimovirus of the family Potyviridae [2] and it is transmitted by the wheat curl mite (WCM) Aceria tosichella Keifer [3], and seeds at a low frequency [4]. Typical symptoms of the WSMV infection in wheat include mosaic and chlorosis, stunting, wrinkled seed and head sterility [5, 6]. Chemicals and agricultural practices are ineffective in WCM control [7]. Furthermore, seed transmission is considered a threat for introducing the virus into virus-free areas, but management of seed transmission probably plays no role in decreasing losses in regions where the virus and its vector are already present [8]. Therefore, deeper knowledge of the genetics of quantitative trait loci (QTLs) for host resistance and putative candidate genes will aid breeders in the development of wheat cultivars with durable resistance against WSMV [9, 10]. Host genetic resistance to WSMV is very narrow and limited to a few QTLs, which are mostly introgressed from wild ancestors of wheat and in some cases are temperature sensitive or associated with linkage drag [9]. To date, four genes associated with resistance to WSMV (Wsm1, Wsm2, Wsm3 and c2652) have been identified. These are located on chromosomes 4DS, 3BS, 7BS, and A or B, respectively [10, 11, 12, 13]. Both Wsm1 and Wsm3, were discovered in Thinopyrum intermedium and transferred into wheat chromosomes in the form of T4DL/4AL*4Ai#2S [14, 15] and T7BS*7S#3L translocations, respectively [16]. The Wsm2 and c2652 genes were identified in common wheat and red spring wheat populations selected in Canada, respectively [8, 17]. Wsm1, Wsm2, Wsm3 and c2652 confer a temperature-sensitive resistance and have much less effect at high temperatures [16, 18]. Lines harboring Wsm1 are resistant to WSMV at 20 °C and postpone symptoms of the disease up to 25 °C, while being susceptible at 28 °C [19]. The lines with the Wsm2 gene are resistant up to 18 °C [20], whereas lines carrying Wsm3 showed effective resistance at 24 °C [16]. Finally, the lines with resistance derived from c2652 expressed resistance at temperatures as high as 28 °C [21]. Introgression of the Wsm1 gene into wheat varieties represents several sources of WSMV resistance, including Mace [22] and KS96HW10-3 [15]. The Wsm2 gene has been introduced into some common wheat varieties, including RonL [23], Snowmass [24], Clara CL [25], Joe [26], Oakley CL [27] and KS Dallas [28]. The Wsm3 gene has been recently incorporated into bread wheat [29] and to date, the c2652 gene has not been used in wheat germplasm development [30]. These genes have all been identified through biparental mapping populations and are limited to a few sources of resistance. The use of Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) offers some specific benefits when compared to bi-parental QTL mapping. GWAS offers higher resolution for QTL identification and captures genetic variation from a broader range of sources [31, 32]. Over the past few decades, genetics-mediated resistance strategies have been widely used in the development of resistance crops through a classical breeding process. However, due to rapid evolution of the pathogen and the interaction with environment, sometimes pathogens are able to overcome this resistance very rapidly. Therefore, there is still a need to identify new sources of resistance [33, 34]. This study aimed to (1) screen a globally diverse panel of 175 wheat genotypes for resistance to WSMV using the mechanical inoculation method, (2) identify QTLs significantly associated with WSMV resistance using the GWAS approach and (3) determine expression profile of key genes identified by GWAS study using RT-qPCR. Germplasm resources evaluated in this study and identified significant QTLs along with candidate genes evaluated through RT-qPCR provide a foundation for future breeding efforts, though independent validation is required before implementation in marker-assisted selection.

sec.title: Plant materials
sec.p: A set of 175 wheat genotypes, including 58 improved Iranian cultivars, 22 international cultivars (often employed in worldwide breeding plans) and 95 accessions from various geographical origins were used in this study (Supplementary Table S1) [35]. The resistant varieties Mace [22] and Snowmass [24], carrying Wsm1 and Wsm2, respectively, and susceptible varieties Marvdasht [36] and Millennium [12] were used as controls.

sec.title: Virus isolate propagation
sec.p: The WSMV isolate was collected from Dolatabad (WSMV-DOLT isolate) in Isfahan province (Accession No. OP903204) and maintained on susceptible genotype Marvdasht [36, 37]. Wheat seeds were sown in pots containing a mixture of peat, perlite and vermiculite (in a ratio of 0.8:1:1), and the pots were subsequently placed in a greenhouse at 25 (± 2) ºC, with a photoperiod of 16 h light and 8 h dark (16 h:8 h) and a relative humidity of 60–70%. The seedlings were mechanically inoculated with WSMV-DOLT isolate at two-leaf stage, following the previously described method [19]. The upper leaves were collected after three weeks and stored at -80 °C until they were used for virus inoculation.

sec.title: Reverse-transcription PCR (RT-PCR) detection of WSMV
sec.p: To detect WSMV, RT-PCR was performed using the WSMVF/WSMVR primer pair [38]. Total RNA was extracted from infected leaves, following the method described by [39]. In RT-PCR, cDNA was synthesized in a 10 µL reaction containing 2 µL of total RNA, 1 µL of 10 µM reverse primer (WSMVR) and 2 µL of DEPC-treated water. After RNA denaturation at 70 °C for 10 min, 2.25 µL of DEPC-treated water, 2 µL of 5× RT buffer, 0.5 µL of 10 mM dNTPs, and 0.25 µL of 200 U/µL M-MuLV reverse transcriptase (Yekta Tajhiz, Iran) were added and the mixture was incubated at 42 °C for 60 min. PCR was performed in a total volume of 10 µL containing 2 µL of cDNA, 5 µL of AMPLIQON 2× master mix, 0.5 µL each of 10 µM forward (WSMVF) and reverse primers, and 2 µL of sterile distilled water. Thermal cycling conditions were as follows: initial denaturation at 95 °C for 10 min; 35 cycles of denaturation at 95 °C for 5 min, annealing at 58 °C for 1 min, and extension at 72 °C for 2 min; followed by a final extension at 72 °C for 10 min. All RT-PCR reactions were performed with three biological replicates.

sec.title: Virus inoculation and phenotyping
sec.p: For each of 175 wheat genotypes, one pot containing six plants was prepared for phenotypic analysis. Plants were grown under controlled greenhouse conditions with a maximum temperature of 17 °C with a 16 h light/8 h dark photoperiod and a relative humidity of 60–70%. This analysis was performed twice (autumn 2020 and autumn 2021), resulting in a total assessment of 12 plants/genotype (six plants per experimental run). The plants were mechanically inoculated as described before [19]. The experiment was conducted in a completely randomized design including several control treatments: non-inoculated plants, mock-inoculated plants, and reference varieties. Specifically, Mace and Snowmass were incorporated as resistant controls while Millennium and Marvdasht were designated as susceptible controls. The wheat genotypes were assessed at 21, 28 and 35 days post inoculation (dpi) [20]. At each time point, individual plants were scored based on symptom severity: 0 for no visible symptoms, 1 for a few chlorotic streaks on only one leaf, 2 for symptoms covering less than 25% of the leaf area, 3 for 25–50% coverage, and 4 for more than 50% coverage. To classify each genotype using data from all 12 plants, the mean symptom score across all plants was used. Genotypes scoring 0 and 1 were grouped as resistant, 2 as moderately susceptible and 3 and 4 as susceptible.

sec.title: Phenotypic data analysis
sec.p: The phenotypic data, which were scored on a scale of 0 to 4 based on symptom severity, were normalized using arcsin square root-transformation [40], and analyzed using a linear mixed model (LMM). In this model, genotype and dpi effects were considered as fixed factors, whereas factor replication and trial were treated as random factors. The broad-sense heritability (h2) was estimated for best linear unbiased estimates (BLUE) values using the formula h2 = σ2g/[σ2g + σ2e/n], where σ2g, σ2e and n are genetic variance, environmental variance and the number of replications, respectively. Subsequently, BLUE values were used to analyze the cluster and correlations and to conduct GWAS. In addition, disease severity scores were analyzed using the principal component analysis (PCA) and visualized by the ClustVis web tool (https://biit.cs.ut.ee/clustvis/) [41], the phenotypic data used in the PCA consisted of disease severity scores obtained from the wheat genotypes. These scores were assessed according to the scoring method as described previously in virus inoculation and phenotyping section at three time points: 21, 28, and 35 (dpi).

sec.title: Genotypic data and genome-wide association study
sec.p: Genomic DNA extraction and genotyping assay using the DArTseq platform (DArT Pty Ltd, Canberra, Australia) of this wheat panel have been described in the previous study [35] which resulted in 94,535 raw DArT-seq markers. The filtering of loci was performed using “dartR” (https://github.com/green-striped-gecko/dartR) version 2.7.2 package in R [35]. To obtain high confidence markers, both SNPs (Supplementary Table S2) and SilicoDArT markers (Supplementary Table S3) were filtered to retain markers with call rates > 90%, reproducibility > 98% and minimum minor allele frequency (MAF) greater than 0.05. Also, markers with unknown chromosome position were removed from the analysis. In total 21,773 high quality polymorphic markers were used for GWAS analysis. To find the best fitting models and reduced false discovery rate (FDR), GWAS was run using three different models; Fixed and random model circulating probability unification (FarmCPU), Bayesian-information and Linkage-disequilibrium Iteratively Nested Keyway model (BLINK) and Multiple Loci Linear Mixed Model (MLMM) implemented in the R package genome association and prediction integrated tool (GAPIT) to identify significant marker-trait association (MTA) [42]. FarmCPU (Fixed and random model Circulating Probability Unification) efficiently controls population structure and kinship by iteratively incorporating associated markers as covariates, reducing false positives while maintaining power in panels with moderate relatedness. BLINK (Bayesian-information and Linkage-disequilibrium Iteratively Nested Keyway) provides computational efficiency and increased power for rare variants by using a more aggressive shrinkage of polygenic effects. MLMM (Multiple Loci Linear Mixed Model) offers a conservative, stepwise forward-backward approach that reduces model overfitting, albeit with higher computational cost. The significance threshold for identifying MTAs was determined using cutoff of p-value < 10− 4 and FDR < 0.05, ensuring a robust control for false positives in the analysis. Map positions of markers showing significant MTAs were identified, corresponding to their genetic positions using the iterative process in a high-resolution DArT-seq consensus map version 4, which contains 105,122 markers distributed across the wheat genome. This genome has three parts (A, B, and D), and each part has seven chromosomes (2n = 6x = 42), (https://www.diversityarrays.com/technology-and-resources/geneticmaps/) and International Wheat Genome Sequencing Consortium (IWGSC) Reference Sequence version 1.04 (IWGSC RefSeq v.1.04) with BLAST+ v2.7.1 [43]. Overlapping markers on the same chromosome for resistance to the WSMV-DOLT isolate were considered as a single QTL when their positions were within 10 cM and showed linkage disequilibrium (LD) with LD r2 > 0.3. Subsequently, in order to compare the QTLs detected in the present study, the map position of significant markers within each QTL was projected onto the two distinct wheat SSR consensus maps [44, 45] to cross-reference them with previously established SSR maps.

sec.title: Candidate gene identification
sec.p: To identify candidate genes associated with different MTAs, the physical positions of markers were aligned to the sequence of the wheat genome assembly IWGSC v.1.0 (https://plants.ensembl.org/Triticum_aestivum/Info/Index). The selection of genomic windows around each MTA was guided by observed linkage disequilibrium (LD) decay patterns in our dataset. LD (measured as r²) declined to a threshold of 0.1, consistent with established GWAS-based gene-mapping approaches [46]. Additionally, a homology search was conducted for MTAs that did not match sequences of encoded proteins in the wheat reference genome. This search was performed using the BLAST tool within the NCBI database. The potential biological functions of genes within significant MTAs were determined through a BLASTP search against the NCBI database using the protein sequences. This approach allowed us to identify similar proteins and assess their association with disease resistance. (https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Blast.cgi). The search criteria were set to require a percent identity greater than 90%, a commonly used threshold for reliable functional prediction in BLASTP analyses. We also evaluated all genotypes for the presence or absence of the resistance allele at each MTA using genotypic and phenotypic data, and generated box plots for each MTA using R to visualize the distribution of trait values among allele classes.

sec.title: Reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR)
sec.p: To elucidate the gene expression of candidate genes associated with SNP markers, RT-qPCR was conducted for two wheat accessions with contrasting response to WSMV infection: IPK41079 with resistance and Alamut being susceptible. Leaf tissues from wheat plants inoculated with WSMV and extraction buffer as mock treatment were collected at 0, 6, 24, 72 h post inoculation (hpi), as well as 20 dpi, and immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen. Total RNA was extracted from 100 mg of frozen plant tissue using an RNA isolation kit (DENA Zist Asia, Iran) and subsequently treated with DNase I enzyme (Fermentas, Life Sciences, Lithuania). The quality of the extracted RNA was assessed by measuring the absorbance values (260 nm/280 nm and 260 nm/230 nm) using the Nanophotometer (Implen, Germany). cDNA was synthesized from 500 ng of total RNA using the M-MLV reverse transcriptase (Yekta Tajhiz, Iran) in a total volume of 20 µl and diluted to 1:32 with DEPC-treated water. Specific primers (Supplementary Table S4) were designed to amplify candidate genes using the sequences downloaded from Ensemble Plants (https://plants.ensembl.org/index.html) and Primer3Plus tools (https://www.bioinformatics.nl/cgi-bin/primer3plus/primer3plus.cgi) and were synthesized by Metabion GmbH. RT-qPCR was conducted in the Step One Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystem, Denmark) using AMPLIQON SYBR Green Master Mix with three biological and two technical replicates for each sample. All reactions were performed in a total volume of 20 µl containing 1X SYBR Green Master Mix, 1 µl of each primer (10 µM) and 2 µl of the 1/32 dilution of the cDNA as template. The PCR condition was 95 °C for 10 min, followed by 40 cycles at 95 °C for 15 s, 60 °C for 30 s and 72 °C for 30 s. After the cycling protocol a melting curve was drawn at 60–95 °C (with a temperature increment of 0.5 °C every 5 s). The melting curves were evaluated to ensure specificity of the amplified products. Data normalization was performed using the Actin gene amplified using specific primer pair Actin Z-F/Actin Z-R (Supplementary Table S4) as the internal control. The relative expression of all genes was calculated using the 2−ΔΔCT method [47].

sec.title: Phenotypic analysis
sec.p: The phenotyping assessment of inoculated wheat plants with six replications indicated that the average scores of disease severity ranged from 0 to 4 (Fig. 1, Supplementary Table S5). In detail, the majority of accessions showed score values of 3 at 28 dpi and 3.5 at 35 dpi, which indicates WSMV susceptibility. At 21 dpi, 90 accessions were scored as susceptible, 48 as moderately susceptible, and 37 showed no symptoms, which were considered as resistant genotypes. At 28 dpi, 158 and seven accessions were susceptible and moderately susceptible to WSMV, respectively and 10 accessions were classified as resistant genotypes (Supplementary Table S5). Finally, at 35 dpi 170 and four genotypes were susceptible and moderately susceptible, respectively, whereas only one highly resistant accession to WSMV, the landrace IPK41079, was identified and remained symptomless at all assessment time points. Our PCA results showed distinct grouping of 175 genotypes as resistant, moderately susceptible and susceptible accessions to WSMV treatment. A total of 147 genotypes clustered with the susceptible control genotypes (Marvdasht and Millennium) in the susceptible group, while the landrace IPK41079 grouped with the resistant control genotypes (Mace and Snowmass). The results indicated the projection of the data on the first two principal components (PC1 and PC2) that represented 93.6% of the total variance (PC1: 76.8% and PC2: 16.8%) (Fig. 2).

sec.p: The RT-PCR results indicated that all tested plants exhibited WSMV infection in their leaves by 35 dpi during the phenotypic assessment. However, the IPK41079 landrace and the resistant controls (Snowmass and Mace), showed no signs of infection both in RT-PCR and phenotypic analyses.

sec.title: GWAS for WSMV resistance in wheat
sec.p: The DArTseq genotypic data used in this study were previously generated and characterized by [35] using the same wheat panel. Population structure analysis in that study revealed three subpopulations based on SilicoDArT markers and four subpopulations based on SNP markers, with no strong clustering by geographical origin. Linkage disequilibrium (LD) decay was estimated at approximately 15 kbp (r² = 0.16). These findings informed our GWAS modeling strategy to control for population stratification [35].

To assess the genetic contribution to the observed phenotypic variation, we estimated the broad-sense h2 for each time point. The calculated values were 0.67 for 21 dpi, 0.65 for 28 dpi, and 0.69 for 35 dpi, indicating a substantial genetic influence on the trait. Since these values are within the acceptable range for conducting GWAS, we proceeded with GWAS analysis using multiple statistical models to ensure robust association detection. Different models (FarmCPU, BLINK, and MLMM) implemented in the GAPIT package were used to test the association between 21,773 DArTseq markers and symptom scores of inoculated plants. A total of 17 significant MTAs were found on 13 different chromosomes for WSMV resistance at 28 and 35 dpi (Table 1). Among the significant identified MTAs, the marker 2254436-32-G/A on chromosome 2B was found by all three models (MLMM, BLINK and FarmCPU). The markers 1133336-57-C/A on chromosome 2 A, 1070207-37-T/C on chromosome 2B, 986698-65-G/T on chromosome 3 A and 1,092,672 on chromosome 6B were identified by two models (Blink and FarmCPU), whereas the remaining MTAs were exclusively identified by a single model (FarmCPU). Two markers were significantly associated with WSMV resistance on each of the chromosomes 2B, 3B, 4B and 7 A, while one marker was found on each of the chromosomes 1B, 2 A, 2D, 3 A, 5 A, 5B, 6 A, 6B and 6D. No markers were found by GWAS for 21 dpi. Only one QTL, located on chromosome 2B, was detected at both 28 and 35 dpi, while the rest were found exclusively at either 28 or 35 dpi, (Table 1; Figs. 3 and 4, Supplementary Figure S1, Supplementary Figure S2, Supplementary Figure S3, Supplementary Figure S4 and Supplementary Figure S5).

sec.p: Examination of the QQ-plots revealed that FarmCPU and BLINK models showed minimal inflation, while MLMM exhibited slight deflation, indicating a more conservative model behavior. These deviations likely reflect the complex population structure of the panel and the ordinal nature of the phenotypic scale, rather than systematic bias, as consensus markers detected across multiple models (e.g., 2254436-32-G/A on chromosome 2B) remained robust.

sec.title: Putative candidate gene identification
sec.p: To identify putative candidate genes underlying resistance to WSMV, we performed a genome-wide analysis of significant MTAs using LD-based genomic intervals. LD decay analysis across wheat chromosomes revealed considerable variation, with physical distances to r² = 0.1 ranging from less than 1 kb to more than 5 Mb (Supplementary Table S6). To accommodate this heterogeneity and ensure robust candidate gene coverage, three window sizes of 100 kb, 500 kb or 1 Mb were selected to flank each significant MTA for candidate gene discovery. Significant MTAs were physically anchored to the wheat reference genome (Chinese Spring RefSeq v1.0), and gene annotations were retrieved for the defined genomic windows flanking each MTA.

Within the 100 kb window, out of 17 significant MTAs, three did not overlap with annotated protein-coding regions. However, the remaining 14 MTAs co-localized with putative genes, including those encoding proteins previously implicated in plant defense responses. These comprised F-box proteins (FBPs), leucine-rich repeat (LRR) proteins, GroEL-like heat shock proteins 60, cytochrome P450s, UDP-glucuronosyl/UDP-glucosyltransferases (UGTs), and serine/threonine/tyrosine-protein kinases. Expanding the search to 500 kb flanking regions (± 250 kb) identified a total of 143 positional candidate genes. Of these, 12 genes encoded FBPs. Ensembl Plants database searches further revealed 10 genes encoding protein kinases, nine encoding zinc finger proteins, and six members of the NAD (P)-binding domain superfamily. Additional candidates included five sugar transporter genes and three genes each encoding transcription factors (TFs), UGTs, flavin monooxygenase-like enzymes, α/β hydrolases, and pentatricopeptide repeat (PPR) proteins. Moreover, two genes were identified for each of the major facilitator superfamily (MFS) transporters, heat shock protein 70 (HSP70) family proteins, plant antimicrobial peptide and cytochrome P450 within the 500 kb interval. Within the broader 1 Mb interval (± 500 kb), 187 genes were identified. Among these, 21 encoded FBPs, with the highest expression located on chromosome 5B. The candidate gene set also included 19 genes encoding plant lipid transfer proteins and eight genes were identified for both TFs and peptidases. Six genes were annotated as encoding cathepsin propeptide inhibitor domain-containing proteins. Moreover, five UGTs and three genes encoding either NB-ARC domain-containing resistance proteins or glycosyltransferases were observed within 1 Mb of significant MTAs. Additional candidates included five genes each encoding sugar transporters and glycoside hydrolases and four genes each encoding zinc finger proteins and serine/threonine/tyrosine-protein kinases.

sec.title: Expression analysis of candidate genes associated with WSMV resistance
sec.p: It has been demonstrated that trait-associated SNPs are more likely to be associated with gene expression. Therefore, the relative gene expression levels of eight candidate genes (Supplementary Table S4) harboring significantly associated DArTseq markers were evaluated in two genotypes with contrasting responses to WSMV (IPK41079 as resistant and Alamut as susceptible) using RT-qPCR. We analyzed the presence or absence of resistance-associated alleles across all genotypes at each significant MTA using both SNP and in silico mapping data. According to the results, MTA (Silico) located at position 1,104,744 on chromosomes 6 A associated with TraesCS6A02G026000 (FBP) was of particular interest due to the clear allelic contrast between resistant (G126 = IPK41079) and susceptible (G56 = Alamut) genotypes (Supplementary Figure S6, Supplementary Figure S7). These findings are summarized in two supporting tables that list the allelic profiles of all evaluated genotypes at each associated MTAs (Supplementary Table S7, Supplementary Table S8).

The gene expression patterns of both genotypes in response to WSMV at five time points (0, 6, 24, 72 hpi and 20 dpi) are shown in Fig. 5 (A-H). The gene TraesCS6A02G026000 (FBP) had higher transcript accumulation in the resistant genotype than in the susceptible genotype at 0 and 72 hpi (8-and 2-fold, respectively). Despite the expression level of this gene displaying a 7-fold increase in the resistant genotype at 20 dpi compared to 0 dpi, the change in expression of the gene did not significantly differ between the resistant and susceptible genotypes at this time point (Fig. 5A).

sec.p: The candidate gene TraesCS7A02G325000 (GroEL-like heat shock protein 60) consistently exhibited higher expression in the resistant genotype compared to the susceptible one following WSMV infection at all-time points, with the highest expression observed at 6 hpi, reaching a 12-fold increase compared to 0 dpi. (Fig. 5B). TraesCS2A02G527300 (P-loop-containing nucleotide triphosphate hydrolase, P-loop NTPase) demonstrated higher expression in the resistant genotype (IPK41079) compared to the susceptible one (Alamut) from 6 to 72 hpi, with the highest expression observed at 6 hpi (Fig. 5C). Notably, this pattern was reversed at 20 dpi, when expression became higher in the susceptible genotype. Such a reversal is not uncommon and may reflect the pathogen’s ability to suppress or hijack the defense signaling pathway in the susceptible host at advanced disease stages, or a prolonged, futile defense effort in the susceptible plant that coincides with widespread cellular stress and senescence.

TraesCS6B02G422600 (WD40-repeat protein, WDR protein) exhibited differential expression between the resistant and susceptible genotypes at 6, 24, 72 hpi, and 20 dpi. The expression level of this gene increased in resistant genotypes at 6 hpi, although it gradually decreased from 24 hpi until 20 dpi. Nevertheless, it still maintained a significantly higher expression level in the resistant genotype than the susceptible one at these time points (Fig. 5D). The expression level of TraesCS2D02G599000 (Cytochrome P450) increased in the incompatible interaction at 6 hpi, following a decrease at 24 and 72 hpi and 20 dpi. In the compatible interaction, expression levels were lower at 6, 24, and 72 hpi. However, at 20 dpi, the compatible interaction exhibited increased expression compared to earlier time points. Overall, the relative expression level was significantly higher in the resistant accession compared to the susceptible genotype at 6, 24, and 72 hpi, but this pattern reversed at 20 dpi (Fig. 5E). The candidate gene TraesCS2D02G599300 (LRR protein) showed upregulation in both resistant and susceptible genotypes following WSMV infection at 6, 24 and 72 hpi when compared to control samples, but it exhibited higher expression in the resistant genotype relative to susceptible genotype at time points of 24, 72 hpi as well as at 20 dpi (Fig. 5F). The gene TraesCS6D02G323200 (UGT) showed significantly higher expression in the resistant genotype at 6, 24, and 72 hpi (Fig. 5G). The expression pattern of the gene TraesCS3A02G261500 (Reticulon-like protein, RTNLs) revealed that this gene was relatively highly expressed in resistant genotype compared to susceptible one at all-time points, except for 6 hpi (Fig. 5H). Overall, RT-qPCR results demonstrated that the relative expression level of evaluated genes in the resistant genotype was significantly higher than that of the susceptible genotype at most of the investigated time points. These results suggest that the higher expression of candidate genes in resistant varieties was possibly positively associated with resistance to WSMV.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: WSMV is a serious and destructive pathogen of wheat worldwide [1]. Among all control measures for managing WSMV, the use of resistant varieties stands out as the most efficient and environmentally friendly strategy [48]. Given that few WSMV resistance genes have been identified for breeding programs and considering the high mutation rates characteristic in RNA viruses, there is a significant potential for the breakdown of these resistance genes. Thus, continuous screening of wheat germplasm is essential for the identification of novel resistance genes and their subsequent incorporation into wheat cultivars. GWAS and QTL analysis play a pivotal role in unraveling the genetic basis of complex traits, providing valuable insights for crop improvement, disease resistance, and the development of more resilient and productive agricultural systems [49].

Hence, in this study, the response of 175 wheat accessions to WSMV was evaluated using a mechanical inoculation method. Phenotypic data analysis showed that the disease severity of wheat accessions differed ranging from 0 to 100%, in an increasing manner from 21 to 35 dpi. The landrace IPK41079 was found to exhibit complete resistance, while Kaveh, Khazar, IPK40501 and TRI10974 accessions displayed moderate susceptibility to WSMV. The remaining wheat accessions showed susceptibility to WSMV.

Moreover, we conducted GWAS on the panel of 175 wheat accessions to identify genomic loci associated with WSMV resistance. Our analysis identified 17 QTLs linked to WSMV resistance at 28 and 35 dpi. Specifically, two markers were located on each of chromosomes 2B, 3B, 4B, and 7 A, while single markers were identified on chromosomes 1B, 2 A, 2D, 3 A, 5 A, 5B, 6 A, 6B, and 6D. Notably, no significant MTAs were detected at 21 dpi, despite 37 accessions showing no symptoms at this early time point. We suspect that most of these accessions experienced delayed viral establishment rather than possessing true genetic resistance, as the vast majority eventually developed symptoms by 35 dpi. In other words, early asymptomatic phenotypes may be transient and unreliable for genetic dissection, which is why our GWAS captured meaningful associations only at later time points when the transcriptional defense response had fully unfolded. The QTLs identified in this study appear to be distinct from the well-established QTLs associated with WSMV resistance, such as Wsm1, Wsm2, and Wsm3 [10, 11, 12, 13]. To critically assess this claim of novelty, we compared the physical positions of our significant markers with the known genomic intervals of these reported genes. Wsm2 has been fine-mapped to the distal end of chromosome 3BS within a 4.0 Mbp interval spanning 15.0–19.0 Mbp in the IWGSC RefSeq v1.0 assembly [17, 20, 30, 50, 51]. Our significant marker on chromosome 3B (1128927-47-C/T) resides at 192,028,551 bp, approximately 173 Mbp away from the Wsm2 interval, confirming it represents a genetically independent locus. Likewise, Wsm1 is located on the short arm of chromosome 4D as a wheat–Thinopyrum intermedium translocation [15, 20, 52], whereas our two markers reside on chromosome 4B, a homologous but distinct chromosome. Similarly, Wsm3 resides on chromosome 7BS [16, 30,53], while our two markers are located on chromosome 7 A. For the remaining QTLs on chromosomes 1B, 2 A, 2B, 2D, 3 A, 5 A, 5B, 6 A, 6B, and 6D, no major WSMV resistance genes have been previously documented. Collectively, these comparisons provide strong evidence that all 17 QTLs identified in this study represent previously unreported genetic loci associated with resistance to WSMV. Chromosome 2B appears to be a hotspot, warranting further investigation into candidate genes in this region. These QTLs will significantly enhance our understanding of the genetic mechanisms underlying WSMV resistance. By integrating genetic and physical maps within the confidence intervals of these identified QTLs, we identified 33 potential candidate genes. Comprehensive literature searches further supported the roles of these genes in disease resistance (Table 1).

We assessed the expression profiles of candidate genes identified by GWAS, including genes encoding LRR protein (TraesCS2D02G599300), P-loop NTPase (TraesCS2A02G527300), FBP (TraesCS6A02G026000), GroEL-like heat shock protein 60 (TraesCS7A02G325000), WDR protein (TraesCS6B02G422600), UGT (TraesCS6D02G323200), cytochrome P450 (TraesCS2D02G599000) and RTNLs (TraesCS3A02G261500), using RT-qPCR. All candidate genes exhibited high expression in the resistant accession (IPK41079) but not in the susceptible accession (Alamut), suggesting their potential roles in defense against WSMV infection.

The TraesCS2D02G599300 and TraesCS2A02G527300 genes encode proteins characterized by a nucleotide-binding site and leucine-rich repeat (NBS-LRR) domains known as NLR protein and P-loop NTPase, respectively. Numerous dominant resistance (R) genes encode NBS-LRR proteins that specifically recognize pathogen effectors and initiate signaling cascades as part of the plant immune response [54, 55]. The NBS-LRR proteins are characterized by a central nucleotide-binding (NB) domain, which is part of the P-loopNTPase superfamily [56, 57]. Wsm1 and wsm2 genes, similar to TraesCS2D02G599300 gene, belongs to the category of dominant resistance (R) genes that encode NBS-LRR protein [10, 22]. Wheat cultivars resistant to WSMV harboring wsm1 and wsm2 effectively block the long-distance movement of the virus through the phloem. However, despite this resistance, virus replication and cell-to-cell movement are still facilitated in these resistant cultivars, occurring at levels comparable to those observed in susceptible cultivars [58]. Consistent with previous studies, maximal expression of this gene occurred at 24 and 72 hpi, the two-time points crucial for the early wheat defense response to barley yellow dwarf virus (BYDV) [59]. P-loop plays a crucial role in binding and hydrolyzing ATP or GTP, acting as a molecular switch that regulates the activation state of the resistance protein. Several of these P-loop NTPase resistance proteins exhibit specific recognition of plant viruses, thereby providing enhanced resistance against such pathogens. The TraesCS2A02G527300 gene (P-loop NTPase) was upregulated in the resistant wheat accession IPK41079, mirroring the expression patterns of RGCLc28 in resistant tomato varieties after tomato leaf curl New Delhi virus (ToLCNDV) infection [60].

The TraesCS6A02G026000, an FBP gene, revealed differential expression patterns between resistant and susceptible accessions, suggesting a link to WSMV resistance. F-box proteins play a pivotal role at the intersection of host anti defense and viral counter-defense. They tightly regulate the levels of NLR immune receptors and argonaute proteins, enabling defense activation only upon pathogen attack while preventing harmful autoimmunity [61]. A notable example of the involvement of F-box proteins in plant antiviral defense is the N gene-mediated resistance against tobacco mosaic virus (TMV). In TMV-resistant Nicotiana benthamiana plants, silencing of NbSGT1 (a highly conserved component of the SCF (Skp1-Cullin-F-box) E3 ubiquitin ligase complex) or NbSKP1 (the SKP1 orthologue in N. benthamiana) compromises the resistance conferred by the N gene. This finding demonstrated that the SCF ubiquitin ligase machinery and its associated complexes play a critical role in the activation of NLR (nucleotide-binding domain and leucine-rich repeat) immune receptors [62]. Conversely, viruses have evolved their own FBPs to target and degrade AGO1, the core effector of antiviral RNA silencing. The P0 of beet western yellows virus (BWYV) and cucurbit aphid-borne yellows virus (CABYV) targeting the RNA silencing machinery by degradation of AGO1 through an autophagy-related pathway [63].

The TraesCS7A02G325000 gene encodes GroEL-like heat shock protein 60 which is classified as HSPs. Although reduced expression of HSPs has been observed in some pathogens, increased expression of HSPs has also been reported in response to many pathogens. The roles of HSPs in plant-virus interactions are complex and multifaceted, as they can both promote viral infection and contribute to plant defense responses. For instance, upregulation of HSPs was found to strongly suppress infection by rice black streaked dwarf virus (RBSDV) in rice [64]. The RTM2 gene, which encodes a small heat shock-like protein restricts the movement of tobacco etch virus (TEV) in Arabidopsis. Unlike typical plant small HSPs, the RTM2 protein is not induced by heat nor involved in thermotolerance; instead, its N-terminal region shares similarity with small HSPs [65]. In a study on potato virus Y (PVY) in heat-tolerant and heat-sensitive potato cultivars demonstrated that HSP expression is induced under both high and low-temperature stress conditions [66]. Additionally, a correlation was observed between the rapid induction of HSP70 genes and improved resistance against Blumeria graminis in barley [67]. Likewise, tomato accession resistant to Phytophthora parasitica showed upregulation of HSPs than susceptible accessions [68].

The TraesCS6B02G422600 gene encodes a WDR protein, which plays roles in immune responses and the activation of pathogenesis-related gene expression [69, 70]. The defining feature of WDR proteins is the presence of a 40 amino acid motif that typically ends with tryptophan (W) and aspartate (D) [71, 72]. The expression profiling of this gene revealed significant variation in response to WSMV infection, suggesting its potential involvement in resistance to pathogens. WDR proteins play multifaceted roles in plant antiviral immunity. It was indicated that in infected plants with cucumber mosaic virus (CMV) and turnip mosaic virus (TuMV), WDR protein positively regulates antiviral defense by promoting programmed cell death and modulating hormone signaling pathways, acting independently of salicylic acid [73].

The higher expression of TraesCS6B02G422600 was evidenced in resistant accession at 6, 24 and 72 hpi, respectively, suggesting that the responses of WDR proteins to WSMV infection occur at the early stage of infection. These results are similar to another study, in which the early stage is considered the main stage of the plant defense response to biotic stresses [74]. It was indicated that the expression of certain genes, including the WDR gene, is more markedly upregulated in incompatible interactions than in compatible ones in resistant and susceptible legume cultivars, following mungbean yellow mosaic India virus (MYMIV) infection [75].

The TraesCS6D02G323200 encodes a UGT. The UGTs form a large enzyme superfamily responsible for transferring sugar residues in higher plants. The members of this superfamily play a critical role and highly specific in resistance against plant viruses by activating the pathogenesis-related (PR) genes [76], detoxifying xenobiotics [77], and regulating salicylic acid (SA), jasmonate (JA), and phenylpropanoid signaling pathways [78, 79, 80]. In N. tabacum a specific group of UGTs known as TOGTs (tobacco glucosyltransferases) confers antiviral resistance by participating in both direct antiviral defense and the regulation of oxidative stress during the hypersensitive response (HR), primarily through the glucosylation of phenylpropanoid compounds [81].

The TraesCS2D02G599000 gene encodes cytochrome P450, belongs to the largest enzymatic protein family (CYP superfamily) in plants. These proteins are known to participate in the response of plants to various biotic and abiotic stresses through detoxification routes and biosynthesis pathways of various defensive compounds such as hormones, fatty acids, and cell wall components [82]. The studies also revealed that the expression of cytochrome P450 is significantly induced in resistant cultivars following inoculation with various pathogens highlighting the stress-responsive of CYP family members in different plant species [83, 84].

Unlike, classical resistance (R) genes that directly recognize pathogen effectors, cytochrome P450 enzymes are essential components of the plant antiviral defense system. They contribute significantly to plant antiviral responses through a range of interconnected roles, including the biosynthesis of phytoalexins, hormone signaling, management of reactive oxygen species (ROS), and the production of secondary metabolites. The cytochrome P450 participates in phenylpropanoid pathway reactions that supply precursors for salicylic acid and hydroxycinnamic acid amide, both of which contribute to active defense against pathogens [85]. Align with this, the high expression level of TraesCS2D02G599000 in IPK41079 accession further confirms its possible potential role in WSMV resistance.

Reticulon-like proteins in plants (RTNLBs) are a family of membrane-shaping proteins which predominantly localized in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). They contribute indirectly to resistance pathways by playing important roles in ER tubulation, desmotubule formation and the regulation of endomembrane trafficking within and between plant cells [86]. Many of viruses facilitate their movement through plasmodesmata (PD) by interacting with the cortical ER or integral ER membrane proteins such as RTNLBs. These interactions may disrupt the desmotubule scaffold [86, 87]. Additionally, its role appears to enhance the activity of immune receptors as demonstrated by similar protein functions observed in other plant species [88]. The comparison of expression patterns indicated that TraesCS3A02G261500 (RTNLs) may be positively related to WSMV resistance in the resistant wheat accession due to its upregulation. Similarly, a comparative transcriptome analysis of two chickpea cultivars, resistant and susceptible to Fusarium oxysporum demonstrated that the resistant cultivar exhibited the highest expression level of RTNLs [89].

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: The limited availability of resistant genetic resources and plant varieties hinders the effective utilization of resistant varieties as a powerful tool in viral disease management. In the present study, phenotypic analysis of a panel of bread wheat genotypes for resistance to WSMV-DOLT isolate showed that most cultivars and landraces were susceptible, while IPK41079 (originated from Romania) was fully resistant to WSMV. Despite the moderate sample size and complex population structure of this panel, the use of multiple GWAS models and high heritability estimates (0.65–0.69) enabled confident detection of 17 moderate-to-large effect QTLs associated with WSMV resistance. Most of identified significant MTAs for WSMV resistance traits using GWAS were associated with diverse plant immune functions against pathogens. The RT-qPCR results showed a distinct upregulation of genes, corresponding to significant MTAs in WSMV-resistant accession IPK41079 compared to Alamut following infection, which underscores the potential pivotal roles of these genes in orchestrating a robust defense response. The identification of these QTLs/genes will aid in characterizing unknown WSMV resistance mechanisms and facilitate breeding applications by providing the molecular foundation underlying resistance. In addition, the identified candidate genes serve as a valuable genetic resource for further research into molecular mechanisms underpinning virus resistance in wheat plants. While our greenhouse-based phenotyping provided precise and reproducible data under controlled temperatures, we acknowledge that field trials across multiple locations and years would further validate the identified QTLs under natural environmental variation. Future studies could include multi-location field trials with natural WSMV infection to confirm the stability and breeding utility of these QTLs. Our data lay the foundation for the identification of markers linked to resistance genes, ultimately facilitating the discovery of resistance genes, a crucial step in effectively controlling this disease.
